The town of Aldermere sits where the river bends around a low hill, and the first written record of it is a grant of fishing rights copied into a register sometime in the 1100s. For most of its history the settlement was small. The parish records, kept in a locked chest behind the altar, rarely name more than forty households in a single year, and the same surnames repeat so often that later historians have had trouble telling one generation from the next. The marsh to the north was drained in stages, and each stage left a different pattern of ditches that can still be traced from the air on a dry evening.

Farming paid for the church tower. Wool paid for the roof. When the wool trade declined, the town turned to the river, and for a while barges carried timber down to the coast and brought back coal, salt and iron. The wharf was rebuilt twice after floods. The second rebuilding is described in a letter that survives in the county archive, though the writer complained more about the price of nails than about the damage.

A fire in 1712 destroyed most of the houses on the north side of the market square. The rebuild was slow because the manors disagreed about who should pay for the new well. By the time the well was finished, the market had moved to the wide street behind the inn, where it remained until the railway arrived. The station was built a mile out of town, which the shopkeepers resented for a generation.

The school opened in a converted barn and moved twice before the county took it over. Its logbooks record epidemics, snow days, and the names of children who left early to work on the farms. One headmaster filled three notebooks with weather observations, and those notebooks are now the best source for the rainfall of the 1830s. He also noted the arrival of the first steam threshing machine, which he described as noisy, expensive and probably temporary.

The guide pauses in the side chapel, where a medieval fresco of the Last Judgment survived the Reformation because it was whitewashed rather than scraped away, and the museum labels the panel beside it the finest Renaissance masterpiece in the county. Visitors often miss it, since the chapel is unheated and opens only in summer.

The river flooded again in 1947 and in 1968. After the second flood a concrete wall was built along the lower bank, and the meadows behind it were turned into playing fields. The allotments moved uphill. The last barge traffic ended in the 1950s, though the wharf itself was not filled in until much later, and its outline is still visible beside the car park.

The population grew quickly after the war. New streets were laid out on the drained marsh, and the school was enlarged twice. A bypass was proposed in the 1970s, debated for a decade, and finally built; the traffic on the high street fell, and the shops that had survived the years of congestion closed one by one. The market shrank to a few stalls on Saturdays.

Today the parish council publishes a newsletter four times a year. It reports on bins, potholes, the Christmas lights and the state of the footpaths along the river. The tone is cheerful and the sentences are short. Most of the back page is taken up with a list of coffee mornings and a reminder that the village hall can be hired for meetings and family gatherings.
